svg.text: Estimating the delay from pairs of consecutive releases
Toy data: onset days 1 to 6, delays 0 to 3, five daily releases R1 to R5 with cut-off days 2 to 6.
New cases reported at each delay
Day 1 is first seen in R1 at age 1, so its delay 0 and 1
cases arrive together as 7 (4 + 3). It is left-truncated.
Each release fills one diagonal. Rows are onset days.
The same triangle, cumulative along each row
Factor from delay 1 to 2 = column sums over those rows
Every row must be seen from delay 0. R 0.2.2 refuses the hatched cell:
“NA values should only appear in the bottom right portion of the triangle”.
So day 1 is dropped, with all of its later growth.
Each release is a snapshot of cumulative cases by onset day.
Days seen in both give later / earlier at each age a:
log(Σ later / Σ earlier) = g(a) + … + g(a + s − 1)
s is the gap in days. Pairs with the same gap are summed by age first.
Each equation is weighted by Σ earlier, and g ≥ 0 (non-negative least squares).
Here s = 1, so exp g(a) is the chain ladder factor.
Dropping day 1 gives panel 2 exactly. Keeping it adds its growth.
28 onset days, releases on days 14, 21 and 28, delays up to D = 14.
Seen at age 0: days 14, 21, 28 only, 3 of 28. R1 backfills
days 1–13 at once. None has a full row. Day 14 is seen only
log(Σ later / Σ earlier) = g(a) + … + g(a + 6), with g = 0 from D on
Most onset days are first seen late, so the chain ladder has no full row.
Release pairs use every day seen in two releases within D.
